rapidly with distance from the wall than it would in the case of constant bulk velocity. Eq. (4) highlights that shear stress reduction in
the vicinity of the wall cannot occur as long as the flow is in the liquid phase (i.e. it can be considered incompressible) because in that
case ub is constant (i.e. it comes from the mass conservation principle for a constant cross section tube), whatever is the incoming
heat transfer rate.
The typical shear stress behavior in a circular cross-section channel with the numerical model developed in [19] is shown in Fig. 6
in non-dimensional form for different fluids and flow regimes. In
case of an incompressible fluid with constant properties, the shear
stress has a linear trend, from - = �w at wall to - = 0 at the tube
axis. Different is the case of a compressible fluid. In fact, bulk velocity changes according to the bulk density reduction, which is the
result of the pseudo-boiling. The higher the heat transfer rate, the
higher will be the pseudo-gas production rate at the wall, and as a
consequence the bulk density reduction and bulk velocity increase.
Therefore, according to Eq. (4), a high heat transfer rate, once the
pseudo-boiling phenomenon is taking place, implies a shear stress
reduction, up to negative values, and thus a major loss of turbulent energy. It is interesting to compare the results obtained at
different heat transfer rates. If one considers moderate heat transfer a shear stress reduction occurs because dub/dx - 0, but it is
not sufficient to cause negative values. The behavior of the shear
stress has an evident influence on the velocity profile as shown
in Eq. (3); for instance, when the shear stress is zero the velocity
presents a peak value. The velocity profiles corresponding to the
shear stress distributions shown in Fig. 6 are presented in Fig. 7 in
non-dimensionalized form with respect to the velocity at the symmetry axis (� = R). According to this point of view, when the heat
transfer rate to a supercritical fluid is large enough, the flow velocity
increases near the wall more than in the high-density core region:
the velocity profile is modified in such a way that large region of
low shear stress are present and thus heat transfer deterioration
occurs.
